data.accessible-tagged-pdf#Accessible, tagged:
Since v0.12.0 the vector PDF is tagged. It carries its logical structure, which a screen reader reads in order, as it reads a web page:
In the deck In the PDF a slide a section (Sect) # … ###### H1 … H6 a paragraph, a list, a table P; L with each item’s label and body; Table, header cells with their scope a link a Link, its clickable area included, its text as its description an image a Figure with its alt text; ![](…) with no alt text is decoration $…$, $$…$$ a Formula, its TeX source as its description code Code, without its line numbers or callout discs a span in that language backgrounds, borders, page numbers artifacts, which a reader skips speaker notes (--pdf-notes) annotations in the structure The file declares PDF/UA-1, the standard for accessible PDF. It carries the deck’s title, which the viewer shows, and its lang (--lang when the deck sets none, en otherwise).
A deck checked with veraPDF passes PDF/UA-1, unless its own headings break the standard’s order. PDF/UA asks that the first heading be an H1 and that no level be skipped (# then ###). Only the deck’s author can fix that. Chrome’s PDF of the same deck, which marp-cli writes, is tagged too, but fails seven of PDF/UA’s rules, has no section per slide and no formulas.
Tagging the 100-slide benchmark deck costs 4% in size (788 against 757 KiB) and no measurable time. --pdf-tags=false writes the PDF without tags.
data.commands#Commands: Command What it does build writes the presentation as HTML, or as a PDF or images (see below). The default: slides deck.md is slides build deck.md expand prints the deck as plain Marp Markdown: templates expanded, kinds replaced by the directives they stand for notes prints the speaker notes kinds lists the kinds the deck can use and what they set; --json (in v0.6.0) writes them as [{"name", "extends", "directives": [{"key", "value"}]}], extends resolved themes lists the themes version prints the version (so does slides --version) completion prints a shell completion script: bash, zsh, fish or powershell slides --help prints the flags of a command. Flags may come before or after the deck: slides deck.md -o out.html and slides -o out.html deck.md are the same. Long flags take two dashes (--html); -o is the only short one. build writes deck.html beside deck.md unless -o says otherwise.
data.configuration-files#Configuration files: marp-cli reads its options from a file in the working directory, and so does slides, when the file is data: .marprc (YAML, JSON is YAML too), .marprc.json, .marprc.yaml, .marprc.yml, .config/marprc*, or the marp key of package.json; --config-file (-c) names any JSON or YAML file, marp.config.json for one. Only the working directory is searched, not its parents, as marp-cli’s search does. A file of JavaScript or TypeScript (marp.config.js …) is a program, which slides does not run: it says so and goes on. The options are those of marp-cli’s documentation that mean something here: title, description, author, keywords, url, ogImage, lang, theme, themeSet, html, allowLocalFiles, template, bespoke, inputDir, output, parallel, pdf, pptx, notes, pdfNotes, pdfOutlines, images, image, imageScale, jpegQuality, watch, server, preview; paths are relative to the file. The command line wins. engine, options and browser* need Marp’s engine and a browser, and are ignored with a warning, as are the --browser* flags: scripts written for marp-cli keep working. (slides.yaml and slides.hcl, with the kinds and the template data, are separate and read as before.)
data.editable-pptx-and-odp#Editable PPTX and:
Since v0.5.0 the slides of a PPTX or an ODP are editable — marp-cli’s PPTX is one picture a slide, and its experimental --pptx-editable converts a PDF through LibreOffice. Here each slide is drawn from its layout, the one the PNG and PDF exports draw:
every line of text is a text box at its laid-out position, in the fonts the slide was laid out with — embedded in the file, so it looks the same on a machine without Lato or Inter (checked with LibreOffice 25.8) — with bold, italic, colours, letter spacing and clickable links; backgrounds, borders and rounded boxes are shapes; gradients are gradient fills in the PPTX and pictures in the ODP (an ODF gradient has two colours); pictures are stored once, however many slides show them; what a slide cannot express — an element under opacity, a filter, a blurred shadow, a formula — is a picture of that element, its text kept over it. Rendered back by LibreOffice, a slide is within 0.04–2 % of the PNG export’s pixels. --pptx-raster and --odp-raster keep one picture a slide.
data.flags#Flags: Flag Commands What it does -o, --output file build, expand, notes output file; - for standard output -I, --input-dir dir build convert the Markdown files under dir, recursively (in v0.6.0); see below -P, --parallel n build decks built at once (in v0.6.0): 5 by default, at most the number of cores; 1 builds them one after the other -w, --watch build build again when a deck, a theme, kinds or data file or the configuration changes, and reload the open pages (in v0.6.0); see below -s, --server dir build serve a directory, converting its decks on request (in v0.6.0); see below -p, --preview build open the result in the default browser (in v0.6.0): the HTML pages with --watch (implied), the server with --server --host addr build the address --server listens on, 127.0.0.1 by default (in v0.6.0) --allowed-host name build a reverse proxy’s public host name that --server answers to, repeatable (after v0.13.0); see Self-hosting --template bespoke|bare build the HTML page’s template (in v0.6.0): bespoke, the default, with the presenting script, on-screen controller and transitions, or bare, the slides stacked (--bare) --bespoke.osc, --bespoke.progress, --bespoke.transition build the bespoke template’s options, with marp-cli’s defaults (in v0.6.0): controller on, progress bar off (it was always drawn before), transitions on; --bespoke.osc=false turns one off -c, --config-file file, --no-config-file build marp-cli’s configuration file, JSON or YAML (in v0.6.0); see below. --config is slides’ own file --browser, --browser-path, --browser-protocol, --browser-timeout build accepted and ignored with a warning (in v0.6.0): there is no browser --pptx-editable, --no-parallel build marp-cli’s spellings of --pptx and -P 1 (in v0.6.0) --config file all configuration file; by default slides.yaml next to the deck, if there is one --no-config all do not read a configuration file --theme-set path all a theme CSS file, or a directory of them (repeatable) --kinds file all a YAML file of kinds (repeatable) --data file all a YAML or JSON file of template data (repeatable) --set key=value all one template value (repeatable) --no-template all do not expand Go templates --strict-yaml all parse directives as strict YAML, as plain Marpit does (Marp Core parses them loosely) --no-emoji all leave :shortcodes: and Unicode emoji as text instead of drawing them as images (since v0.4.0: Emoji) --html build allow all raw HTML; by default, Marp Core’s allowlist --lang code build the page’s lang when the deck sets none --bare build stack the slides, without the presenting script --pdf build write a PDF, one page per slide, with an outline — text and shapes as vectors (also chosen by -o file.pdf) --pdf-raster build write the PDF with each page one image of the slide, as v0.3.0 did --notes build write the speaker notes as a text file, slides separated by --- as marp-cli does (in v0.6.0; also chosen by -o file.txt). The notes command prints them in another layout --pdf-notes build add each slide’s speaker notes to its PDF page as a note annotation, as marp-cli does (in v0.6.0). Asks for a PDF when nothing else says what to write --pdf-outlines, --pdf-outlines.pages, --pdf-outlines.headings build the PDF’s bookmarks (in v0.6.0): “Page N” per slide and the headings nested under it. On by default here, unlike marp-cli; =false turns one off. See below --images png|jpeg build write one image per slide: deck.001.png, … --image png|jpeg build write the first slide as an image (also chosen by -o file.png or -o file.jpg) --pptx build write a PowerPoint file with its speaker notes (also chosen by -o file.pptx): editable since v0.5.0, one picture per slide in v0.4.0 --pptx-raster build write a PowerPoint file of one full-slide picture per slide, as marp-cli does (since v0.5.0); --image-scale defaults to 2 --odp build write an OpenDocument presentation with its speaker notes (also chosen by -o file.odp): editable since v0.5.0 --odp-raster build write an OpenDocument presentation of one picture per slide (since v0.5.0) --jpeg-quality n build JPEG quality, 1 to 100 (default 85) --image-scale n build device pixels per CSS pixel for images and PDF (default 1); 2 gives 2560×1440 for 16:9, with text and vectors drawn at that density, not enlarged --allow-local-files build let images and PDF read local files, from under the deck’s directory only; refused by default, as with marp-cli --theme name|file.css build override the deck’s theme (in v0.6.0): a theme name, or a CSS file, which becomes the theme whatever @theme it declares; a directory is refused, use --theme-set --title, --description, --author, --keywords, --url, --og-image build the page’s metadata (in v0.6.0), over the deck’s title, description, author, keywords, url and image directives; see below
data.images-pdf-pptx-and-odp#Images, PDF, PPT: -o with a .pdf, .pptx, .odp, .png or .jpg extension picks the format, as marp-cli does. Output directories are created. A PDF has one page per slide, at the slide’s size, and an outline of the slides and their headings.
data.overview-view#Overview view: In v0.8.0, press o (or Escape: marp-cli toggles with both), the controller’s grid button, or the presenter view’s page counter, and every slide shows whole in a grid over the page. The arrow keys choose a slide (up and down by row), Home and End go to the ends, and the other windows follow; Enter, Space or a click chooses a slide and, over the page, closes the overview. Over the presenter view a choice leaves it open (the presenter picks the slide to show, and keeps looking). The “Close overview” button, o and Escape close it. It is marp-cli’s: the page again in a frame at ?view=overview&sync=KEY, sharing the position through localStorage, with no network. The slides in the grid are focusable and labelled “Slide N”, and the closed overview is inert, so keyboard and screen-reader users never land in it. The two views together add about 15 KB to a page.
data.page-metadata#Page metadata:
The command line wins over the deck, as in marp-cli, where the flags are appended to the deck as one last directive comment. Rules read from marp-cli 4.5.1 and pinned by tests against its output (in v0.6.0): A deck that sets no title takes the text of its first heading of the lowest level, as written (# **Bold** title gives **Bold** title). With no heading there is no .
  • keywords are split at commas, trimmed and deduplicated; a front-matter list is taken as it is. Like marp-cli, the page carries the keywords tag from the second keyword on, not for a single one.
  • An invalid url (not absolute) is ignored with a warning, and the previous value kept; a valid one also writes and og:url.
  • author and description come with their Open Graph twins; og:image:alt and the large Twitter card need both a title and an image.
data.pdf-notes-and-outline#PDF notes and outl:
In v0.6.0 the PDF takes marp-cli’s two options, and they are compared with the PDFs marp-cli 4.5.1 writes for the same deck:
--pdf-notes puts each slide’s speaker notes on its page as a note annotation: a yellow Note icon at the bottom left whose contents are the notes (several comments joined by a blank line) and whose title is the deck’s author. --pdf-notes alone asks for a PDF, as in marp-cli. The outline holds a bold bookmark “Page N” per slide and, under it, the slide’s headings nested by level (--pdf-outlines.pages and --pdf-outlines.headings choose the two). The outline is on by default here and off in marp-cli. slides has always written one; it costs a few hundred bytes and makes a long deck navigable, so the default stays. --pdf-outlines=false, or marp-cli’s --no-pdf-outlines, turns it off, and =false on .pages or .headings drops that part. A heading bookmark jumps to its slide; marp-cli also scrolls to the heading. Rendering is done by go-webengine and the PDF is written by go-pdfkit; the fonts the built-in themes ask for (Lato, Roboto Mono) come from go-opentype/fonts and are embedded, so no render touches the network. There is no Chrome.
--image-scale 2 renders at two device pixels per CSS pixel. Local images are refused unless --allow-local-files is given, and even then only files under the deck’s directory are read: a deck from elsewhere cannot reach ~/.ssh. Several and split backgrounds (![bg left:40%]) render as Marp’s layers do.
--pptx writes the deck with go-ooxml’s WritePresentation, with the speaker notes and the deck’s metadata. Since v0.5.0 the slides are editable (below); --pptx-raster writes one full-slide picture per slide, as marp-cli does, at a scale that defaults to 2 that --image-scale overrides. LibreOffice opens the result. Only LibreOffice was tested; PowerPoint and Keynote were not.
--odp writes an OpenDocument presentation, through go-odf’s WritePresentation, with its speaker notes; --odp-raster writes one picture per slide.
data.planned#Planned: Not built yet: formulas as vectors in the PDF. When they arrive, they are a command or flag here.
data.presenter-view#Presenter view:
In v0.7.0 the page has marp-cli’s presenter view. Press p, or the last button of the controller, and a window opens with the current slide, the step after it, your speaker notes, the page, the time and a timer (click the timer to reset it; + and - resize the notes; the bar between the slides and the notes can be dragged). The two windows follow each other both ways: the arrow keys, a click on the next step or on Previous/Next in either one moves the other, a fragment at a time.
It works as marp-cli’s does, read from its 4.5.1 sources: the window is ?view=presenter&sync=KEY of the same file, the next step is the same page as ?view=next in a frame, and the windows share their position through localStorage (bespoke-marp-sync-KEY), so it needs no server and no network, and does not work in a browser that has no localStorage (the button says so). The notes are text: &, < and > are escaped, so a note can never be markup. They are in the page, hidden, for the presenter view to take, which keeps them out of what a screen reader reads to the audience. --bare pages have none of it. The view adds about 10 KB to a page.
data.several-decks-and-a-directory#Several de:
In v0.6.0 build takes several decks, a directory (the decks under it, found recursively) or a pattern, and builds up to --parallel of them at once. - is standard input; unlike marp-cli, a pipe is not read unless - says so.
A pattern is read as marp-cli’s glob reads it (** and {a,b} in v0.7.0; quote it so that the shell leaves it to slides): *, ?, [a-z] and {md,txt} within a name, ** for any number of directories, so that 'docs/**/*.md' takes the decks of the tree. A wildcard does not reach a name that starts with a dot, nothing is looked for in node_modules, case matters (*.md does not find UPPER.MD), and whatever a pattern matches is converted, whatever its extension. A pattern that matches nothing is an error.
-I dir finds the Markdown files (.md, .mdown, .markdown, .markdn, in lower case) under dir, as marp-cli does: node_modules and dot directories are not looked in. With -o out, each deck is written at its path under dir, mirrored under out: dir/sub/b.md gives out/sub/b.html (b.pdf, b.001.png, b.txt, … whatever the flags say). Without -o the outputs go next to their decks. Naming decks as well as -I is an error, and so is -o file for several decks (-o - is allowed). -P n builds n decks at once. A deck’s own rendering already uses the cores, so n is capped by their number; with -o - decks are built one after the other. The messages of a deck stay together, and a deck that fails does not stop the others: the exit status is 1 and the message lists the failures.
data.slidesyaml#slides.yaml:
A configuration file next to the deck applies to it, so a folder of decks shares one:
kinds: kinds.yaml # a mapping of kinds, or file(s) holding one themes: # theme CSS files or directories - themes/ data: # template data company: Example Inc. html: false # allow all raw HTML lang: en Kinds: the deck’s own kinds: override the file’s and the command line’s. Data: the file’s and the command line’s data override the deck’s front matter, so one deck can be built with different data.
data.transitions-and-the-presenting-page#Tran:
In v0.6.0 the transition directive of marp-cli works: , a name and an optional duration, for the slide and the ones after it, or for one. The built-in names are marp-cli’s: clockwise, counterclockwise, cover, coverflow, cube, cylinder, diamond, drop, explode, fade, fade-out, fall, flip, glow, implode, in-out, iris-in, iris-out, melt, overlap, pivot, pull, push, reveal, rotate, slide, star, swap, swipe, swoosh, wipe, wiper and zoom; none turns it off. The page plays it with the browser’s View Transition API when the viewer leaves the slide that has it, forwards, and when it comes back to it; browsers without the API change slides as before, and a viewer who asks for reduced motion gets a plain fade. A theme can bring keyframes of its own, named marp-transition-NAME (or marp-outgoing- and marp-incoming-, and -backward), which are used before the built-in ones.
The page has the on-screen controller — previous, page, next, full screen — which shows when the pointer or a key moves and hides after a moment (--bespoke.osc=false removes it), and, with --bespoke.progress, a progress bar. The progress bar is off by default now, as in marp-cli; it was always drawn before.
data.vector-pdf#Vector PDF:
Since v0.4.0 the PDF is drawn as vectors: go-webengine paints the laid-out slide into the PDF instead of into pixels. The text is text, in the fonts the slide was laid out with, subset-embedded with a /ToUnicode map — it can be selected, searched and copied. Backgrounds, borders and gradients are paths and shadings, an image shown on many slides is embedded once, and links are clickable. The 100-slide benchmark deck is 758 KiB, against 837 KiB for marp-cli and 10 MiB for the image PDF of v0.3.0, and it is written in 0.3 s.
An element with no vector form here — under opacity < 1, with a filter or a rotation, a blurred box-shadow, a gradient whose opacity fades — is drawn as a bitmap of that element only, its text laid over it invisibly so it stays selectable. Formulas are still bitmaps. --pdf-raster writes one image per page, as v0.3.0 did.
data.watch-serve-and-preview#Watch, serve and:
In v0.6.0, with marp-cli’s routes and live reload protocol (read from its 4.5.1 sources and compared with a running marp -s).
slides --server dir (-s) serves the directory on http://127.0.0.1:8080/ (the PORT environment variable changes the port; a port already in use is an error that says so):
Request Answer /deck.md the deck as HTML, converted on request /deck.md?pdf, ?pptx, ?png, ?jpg (or ?jpeg), ?notes (or ?txt) the deck converted as the query asks; the PPTX is an attachment a directory its index.md or PITCHME.md as a page, else an index with a PDF and a PPTX link for each deck any other file the file a deck that does not convert 503 with the error A page opens a WebSocket to /.__marp-cli-watch-notifier__/, where the id is the SHA-256 of the deck’s path; the server sends ready, then reload when the deck, or anything under the directory, changes. A directory requested without its trailing slash is redirected to it (marp-cli serves its index there, which breaks the page’s relative links).
--watch (-w) builds the decks, then builds again the one that changes and, when a --theme-set file, a kinds or data file or the configuration changes, all of them. The pages it writes open a socket on the loopback (port 37717, or the next free one) and reload when their deck is built again. A deck that fails to build is reported and watched still. --preview (-p) opens the default browser on the server, or on the HTML pages just built; there is no window of its own, since slides has no browser to drive.
The server is a way into the machine, so it is stricter than marp-cli’s, which listens on every interface and checks nothing:
it listens on 127.0.0.1; --host changes that, with a warning, and a wildcard address cannot check the Host header any more; the Host header must be a loopback name (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1], *.localhost) or the host it listens on, which stops DNS rebinding; a WebSocket’s Origin must be the server’s own; the watch mode’s sockets also take the null origin of a page opened from a file; a request from another site that is not a navigation (a script, an image, a fetch) is refused; a path is cleaned, its symbolic links are resolved, and the result must be inside the directory: .. and a link out of it are refused, and so is ?pdf of a deck outside; names that start with a dot (.git, .env) are not served; only GET and HEAD; a few conversions at once; at most 4096 directories watched, and none in node_modules or under a dot. Behind a reverse proxy, --allowed-host name (after v0.13.0, repeatable) adds the proxy’s public name to the accepted Host and Origin; the checks stay on and the server stays on the loopback. Self-hosting puts it behind Caddy, with HTTPS and a sign-in.

data: Emoji are in v0.4.0; v0.3.0 had none. Write an emoji as a shortcode or as the character itself: # Launch :rocket: 🎉 Shortcodes :smile: :+1: :heart_eyes: and Unicode 😄 👍🏽 👩‍💻 🇫🇷 1️⃣. Each becomes the Twemoji image Marp Core draws, with the markup Marp Core writes:
data.attribution#Attribution: The graphics are Twemoji, Copyright 2020 Twitter, Inc and other contributors, licensed CC-BY 4.0 and continued by the jdecked/twemoji project. A deck that shows them should credit them, for instance in a footer or on a closing slide. The shortcode table is markdown-it-emoji’s (MIT).
data.no-network#No network:
Marp Core’s src is a URL on a CDN, so a deck shown offline, printed, or turned into a PDF on a machine without a connection shows broken images. go-slides puts the SVG itself in a data: URI. The graphics (4,009 of them, Twemoji 17.0.3, Emoji 17.0) are embedded in the program from the pure-Go module go-icons/twemoji, 2 MB compressed and read only when a deck has an emoji.
The images are drawn by the HTML page, by --images/--image, by --pdf, by --pptx and by --odp alike: go-webengine rasterizes the SVG. All 4,009 graphics parse and draw under its SVG rasterizer; a test checks it. Since v0.5.0 that rasterizer is go-gfx/oksvg v0.2.0: clipPath, fill-rule: evenodd and arc commands now draw as Chrome draws them, which changed one Twemoji and 211 others, and SVG logos are no longer garbled.
The rule that sizes an emoji to the text (img[data-marp-twemoji], one em square, aligned with the baseline) is added to the theme as Marp Core adds it, so a theme of your own gets it too.
data.turning-it-off#Turning it off: --no-emoji (in code, slides.Config{NoEmoji: true}) leaves shortcodes and Unicode emoji as the text they were written as, which is Marp Core’s emoji: false.
data.what-is-converted#What is converted:
The rules are Marp Core’s; a test compares them with the HTML Marp Core 4.4.0 writes for a deck of every case.
:smile:, :+1:, :heart_eyes: the 1,903 names of markdown-it-emoji, in text, headings, links, tables, header and footer; not in code, URLs or an image’s alt text 😄, 👩‍💻, 🇫🇷, 1️⃣, 👍🏽 Unicode emoji, in text and in code: Marp Core rewrites the rendered code HTML ✔, ©, ™, ▶ stay text: characters whose default presentation is text are emoji only with U+FE0F (✔️); ❤ is the exception ☺︎ stays text: a U+FE0E after an emoji asks for the plain glyph 12:30:45, :not_a_name: stay as written A heading’s id and the outline use the emoji, not the shortcode’s name: # Launch :rocket: has the id launch-%F0%9F%9A%80, as in Marp.
Where go-slides differs from Marp Core, it converts more: ✌️ ☝️ ✍️ 🏋️ and a few other text-default characters that Marp Core’s emoji-regex leaves as text, and the handful of sequences Twemoji draws that Unicode does not list.

data:
Twelve small decks from the examples/ folder of go-slides, each showing one thing well. The thumbnails are the first slide of each deck, rendered by go-slides itself when this site is built; CI builds every deck to HTML and PDF, so none of them breaks.
Open in the playground loads the deck in your browser, in a link that sends nothing to any server. A deck that has files besides deck.md (a kinds file, included parts, images) cannot travel in a link: download its .zip, and import it with the playground’s file panel, or unzip it and build it with slides build --allow-local-files deck.md.
The pictures are original SVGs of the go-slides authors, released under CC0 1.0, and the decks that use them say so.
The default theme 4 slides
Marp's default theme, as a clean light deck for documentation and reports.
Open in the playground Source on GitHub deck.md --- slides: true theme: default paginate: true title: The default theme description: Marp's default theme, as a clean light deck for documentation and reports. footer: go-slides · default theme --- # The default theme A clean, light deck: black text on white, a blue accent, room to breathe. --- ## Headings, lists, quotes - Level-one and level-two headings get a rule under them - **Bold**, *italic*, `inline code` and [links](https://github.com/go-slides/slides) - Lists nest: - like this - and this > A quotation is set apart by a bar on its left. --- ## Tables and code | Theme | Feels like | Best for | | ------- | -------------- | ------------------ | | default | a clean page | documentation | | gaia | a warm poster | talks | | uncover | a calm stage | keynotes | ```go func main() { fmt.Println("hello, slides") } ``` --- <!-- _class: invert --> ## Invert `<!-- _class: invert -->` flips one slide to light-on-dark, whatever the theme. Nothing else changes. The gaia theme 4 slides
Marp's gaia theme, warm and bold, with lead slides for covers and chapter breaks.
Open in the playground Source on GitHub deck.md --- slides: true theme: gaia paginate: true title: The gaia theme description: Marp's gaia theme, warm and bold, with lead slides for covers and chapter breaks. footer: go-slides · gaia theme --- <!-- _class: lead --> # The gaia theme Warm paper, strong headings, a cover slide. --- ## Content slides Gaia sets a heavy heading over a warm background, with a coloured band on the left of ordinary slides. - It reads well from the back of a room - Bullets stay short - One idea per slide --- <!-- _class: lead invert --> ## Lead, inverted The `lead` class centres a slide. Add `invert` for a dark one. --- ## Spot directives A directive with an underscore styles **this slide only**. Without it, the directive carries on to the slides after. ```markdown <!-- _class: lead invert --> # One slide <!-- class: lead --> # This one and the next ones ``` The uncover theme 5 slides
Marp's uncover theme, centred and calm, for keynote-style talks.
Open in the playground Source on GitHub deck.md --- slides: true theme: uncover paginate: true title: The uncover theme description: Marp's uncover theme, centred and calm, for keynote-style talks. footer: go-slides · uncover theme --- # The uncover theme Centred, spacious, quiet. --- ## One thought per slide Uncover centres its content and gives it a lot of white space. It suits few words and big ideas. --- <!-- _class: invert --> ## Dark when you need it `<!-- _class: invert -->` makes this slide dark. --- ## Quotes stand out > A slide is a sentence, not a document. --- # Thank you [github.com/go-slides/slides](https://github.com/go-slides/slides) Slide kinds 6 slides
A slide says what it is (title, chapter, quote) and a kinds file says how each looks.

data.a-first-deck#A first deck:
Any Marp deck is one. Save this as talk.md:
--- marp: true theme: default paginate: true footer: "{{ .talk }}" data: talk: Pure Go slides topics: [Why, How, Next] --- # {{ .talk }} {{ range .topics }} --- # {{ . }} {{ end }} The front matter is Marp’s, plus data:. The body is a Go template: the range writes one slide per topic, each starting with ---, and the first slide is of the built-in kind title (no header, no footer, no page number).
data.build-it#Build it: slides talk.md # writes talk.html beside the deck slides -o slides.html talk.md # or somewhere else; -o - for standard output slides with no command is slides build. Flags may come before or after the deck. Open the HTML in a browser; the keyboard moves between slides.
data.expand-it#Expand it:
slides expand talk.md prints the same deck as plain Marp Markdown (output of main at 4ae5c49, 2026-10-18):
--- marp: true theme: default paginate: true footer: "Pure Go slides" --- # Pure Go slides --- # Why --- # How --- # Next The four slides the range generated, the footer with its value, and the title kind replaced by the spot directives it stands for. Anything that reads Marp — marp-cli, the VS Code extension — can take it from there, so nothing written with go-slides' additions is locked in.
data.export-images-pdf-pptx-and-odp#Export im: slides talk.md --pdf # one page per slide, with an outline slides talk.md --images png # talk.001.png, talk.002.png, … slides talk.md --image jpeg # the first slide only slides talk.md -o out/slides.pdf # the extension picks the format; out/ is created slides talk.md --images jpeg --jpeg-quality 90 slides talk.md --images png --image-scale 2 # 2560×1440 for 16:9 slides talk.md --pdf --allow-local-files # images from under the deck's directory slides talk.md --pptx # or -o talk.pptx, with notes slides talk.md --odp # or -o talk.odp: the same, as OpenDocument No browser is involved: go-webengine renders the slides and go-pdfkit writes the PDF. Local images are refused unless --allow-local-files is given. Since v0.5.0 the slides of a PPTX or ODP are editable — text boxes, shapes and pictures, fonts embedded — where marp-cli’s are pictures; --pptx-raster keeps pictures (Editable PPTX and ODP). Since v0.4.0 the PDF is vectors, its text selectable (v0.3.0 wrote one image per page). See Command line.

Go 1.27.2 or later:
go install github.com/go-slides/slides/cmd/slides@latest slides is one static Go binary with no cgo: nothing else to install, no Node, no Chrome. This page describes v0.13.0.

data:
HCL is in v0.3.0 (go-slides/slides#13). Everywhere slides reads YAML, it also reads the native syntax of HCL2 — for its expressions and its functions.
Where YAML HCL front matter --- … --- ---hcl … --- configuration slides.yaml slides.hcl, looked up first kinds files --kinds kinds.yaml, kinds: kinds.yaml any file named *.hcl data files --data data.yaml or .json any file named *.hcl Directive comments () stay YAML, as in Marp, and the deck body stays a Go template.
data.a-front-matter-in-hcl#A front matter in: ---hcl theme = "gaia" paginate = true title = "Quarterly review" data = { company = "ACME" quarter = 3 } header = format("%s — Q%d", data.company, data.quarter) footer = "${upper(data.company)} · ${page()}/${total()}" date = formatdate("D MMMM YYYY", now()) kind "chapter" { extends = "section" class = ["lead", "invert"] } --- # {{ .title }} Attributes are the YAML keys under the same names: Marp’s directives (theme, paginate, header, footer, class, backgroundColor…), the metadata (title, author…), template, delims, kinds (file paths) and data, an object. kind "" { … } blocks define kinds, with the local directives and extends. Values reach the directives in the string forms YAML gives them — true is "true", a list of classes is a list — so a directive behaves the same whichever syntax set it. null leaves a directive unset. data keeps its types: in templates an integral number is an int, other numbers a float64, and lists and objects stay lists and maps, so {{ add .quarter 1 }} works. An HCL value is final: Go templates do not run over it a second time.
data.errors#Errors:
Errors are HCL’s diagnostics, positioned in the deck file itself: footer = data.compnay on the deck’s fourth line gives
deck.md:4:14: Unsupported attribute: This object does not have an attribute named "compnay".
data.functions#Functions: page(), total() the page number and the last page number, as {{ page }} and {{ total }}: a footer paginates now(), timestamp() the time, RFC 3339, local and UTC; formatdate formats it env(name) an environment variable, "" when unset file(path) a UTF-8 text file of at most 1 MiB, relative to the deck or the configuration file numbers abs ceil floor log max min parseint pow signum strings chomp format formatlist join lower regex regexall regexreplace replace split strlen strrev substr title trim trimprefix trimspace trimsuffix upper collections chunklist coalesce coalescelist compact concat contains distinct element flatten keys length lookup merge range reverse slice sort values zipmap encodings csvdecode jsondecode jsonencode dates formatdate timeadd All but the first four rows are go-cty’s standard library. None reaches the network.
data.licences#Licences: HCL support links hashicorp/hcl (MPL-2.0, used unmodified as a library) and zclconf/go-cty (MIT).
data.marp-and-slides-expand#Marp and slides e:
Marp reads ---hcl as the start of a front matter too — its front-matter rule opens on any first line that begins with three dashes — and, the block not being a YAML mapping, applies none of it: the deck still renders in Marp, without its directives. A test pins this against Marp Core’s own output.
slides expand writes the front matter back as YAML, so the expanded deck is plain Marp and renders as slides renders the original:
--- theme: "gaia" paginate: true title: "Quarterly review" header: "ACME — Q3" footer: "ACME · 1/2" date: "19 October 2026" ---
data.slideshcl#slides.hcl:
kinds = "kinds.hcl" # or a list of files themes = ["themes/acme.css"] data = { company = "ACME" } # or file paths html = false lang = "en" kind "quote" { extends = "blank" footer = "${data.company}" } An unknown attribute is an error, not a silent no-op. A kinds file holds kind blocks; its other attributes are ignored, so slides.hcl can serve as one. A data file’s attributes are the data’s keys:
# data.hcl company = "ACME" year = 2026 motto = trimspace(file("motto.txt"))
data.variables#Variables:
data is the template data: the front matter’s own data, overlaid by slides.hcl’s, by --data files and by --set. "${data.company}" works wherever {{ .company }} would.
Front-matter attributes may reference data.* but not each other: footer = title is an error. Spot directives (_class…) are not HCL identifiers; write them in a comment.

data: A kind is a named preset of local directives: header, footer, pagination, class, background. A slide says what it is — title, section — instead of repeating how it looks, and a deck’s look is changed in one place.
data.built-in#Built in: Kind Sets title class: lead, no page number, no header, no footer section class: lead content nothing: the deck’s own defaults blank no page number, no header, no footer Any of them can be redefined.
data.defining-kinds#Defining kinds:
In the front matter:
--- marp: true kinds: chapter: class: invert backgroundColor: "#1e1b4b" paginate: false quote: extends: blank class: quote --- extends starts a kind from another one’s directives. A kind accepts the local directives and extends.
data.leaving-go-slides#Leaving go-slides: slides expand writes every kind out as the spot directives it stands for, slide by slide, so the result is plain Marp Markdown that any Marp tool reads.
data.sharing-kinds#Sharing kinds:
A team’s kinds belong in one file every deck names:
# kinds.yaml chapter: class: invert paginate: false --- marp: true kinds: kinds.yaml # or a list of files --- or --kinds kinds.yaml on the command line, or kinds: in slides.yaml. The order is: the built-in kinds, then the command line and the configuration file, then the deck’s own kinds:.
slides kinds talk.md lists the kinds a deck can use and what each one sets.
data.using-a-kind#Using a kind: # Part two --- ![bg](photo.jpg) kind: applies like a local directive: to this slide and the ones after it. _kind: applies like a spot directive: to this slide only. Switching kinds first clears what the previous kind set, so a class or a footer never leaks from one kind into the next. Directives written on the slide itself win over the kind.

data: A deck written for Marp is a go-slides deck. The rules below are Marpit’s and Marp Core’s; where go-slides differs, this page says so.
data.around-the-slide#Around the slide: Header and footer: header: and footer: directives, in Markdown. Pagination: paginate: true. Speaker notes: an HTML comment that is not a directive is a note. slides notes prints them. Fragmented lists: a list written with * (or 1)) appears item by item, as in Marp.
data.directives#Directives: Kind Where Applies to global front matter, or anywhere the whole deck: theme, style, headingDivider, lang… local this slide and the ones after it spot (underscore) this slide only The local directives are Marpit’s: paginate, header, footer, class, backgroundColor, backgroundImage, backgroundPosition, backgroundRepeat, backgroundSize, color. Directives are parsed as loose YAML, as Marp Core does; --strict-yaml parses them as plain Marpit does.
data.images#Images: ![bg](image.jpg) makes an image the slide’s background, with Marp’s keywords: bg contain, bg cover, bg 50%, bg left/bg right for a split background, several bg images side by side, and the image filters (blur, sepia, grayscale…). Inline image sizes (w:200px, h:) are read as Marp reads them.
data.slides#Slides: A horizontal ruler — --- on a line of its own, as Marpit splits — starts a new slide, and so does a heading of the level the headingDivider directive names. The front matter, between the first two ---, holds global directives and the deck’s data.
data.themes#Themes: default, gaia and uncover are built in, selected with theme:. A theme of your own is a CSS file with Marp’s /* @theme name */ comment, given with --theme-set or listed under themes: in slides.yaml.
data.where-go-slides-differs#Where go-slides: Templates. {{ }} in the body is a Go template action (see Templates). A deck that shows {{ as text outside a code block needs --no-template, or the text escaped as Go templates escape it. Code blocks and code spans are left alone. Kinds. kind: and _kind: are directives Marp does not have (see Kinds). slides expand replaces them with the directives they stand for, so the expanded deck is plain Marp. Outputs. HTML, PNG, JPEG, PDF, PPTX and ODP, through Go libraries rather than a headless browser (see Command line for the known limit). In v0.4.0, as in marp-cli, a PPTX holds pictures; since v0.5.0 its slides are editable text boxes and shapes, --pptx-raster keeping the pictures. Fitting headings. # Title is supported: the heading fills the slide width on one line, in the page and in every export. Math and code. $…$ and $$…$$ follow Marp Core’s delimiter rules and are typeset by go-tex/math; fenced code is highlighted by go-rouge with highlight.js class names (see Math and code).

data: Math and code are in v0.2.0.
data.code#Code:
Fenced code blocks are coloured by go-rouge, which writes highlight.js class names, the ones Marp’s themes style:
```go fmt.Println("hello") ``` A language go-rouge does not know is written as plain text, as Marp Core does.
data.code-callouts#Code callouts:
In v0.8.0 a code line can end with a numbered disc that refers to a note below the block. The syntax is Quarto’s, which is also Asciidoctor’s comment form. The marker is a comment in the code’s own language, so the code stays valid, and the notes are the ordered list right after the block:
```go func main() { // <1> x := load() // <2> fmt.Println(x) } ``` 1. The entry point. 2. Reads the input. Write Means // <1>, # <1>, -- <1>, ; <1>, % <1>, ' <1> a line comment that holds only the marker: both are replaced by the disc , /* <1> */ the same, for languages with wrapped comments // <1> <2> two discs on one line x = 1 # count <1> the comment’s text stays and the disc follows it The markers become discs only when the list right after the block starts at 1 and has an item for every number. Otherwise the block stays as written. The discs are rings in the code’s colour, in the default, gaia and uncover themes, light or dark. The list’s items are numbered with the same discs.
The discs are not selectable. Copying the code from the page gives the code without its markers. In a PDF they are vectors left out of the text, and in a PowerPoint or OpenDocument file they are editable shapes. Callouts combine with line numbers. Marp Core has no callouts (marp-core 4.4.0), so in Marp the comments and the numbered list show as written. A deck that does not use them renders as before, to the byte.
In v0.9.0, a disc and its note find each other in the HTML page. Hovering a disc, or reaching it with Tab, tints its note, and a note does the same for its disc. This is what Quarto’s code-annotations: hover does, but here the style sheet does it alone, with no script. It therefore works the same in the playground’s sandboxed preview and in VS Code’s preview, which both restrict scripts. Each disc is described by its note, so a screen reader reads the note when it reaches the disc. The tint fades in only when the reader has not asked for reduced motion. Images, PDF, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files are unchanged, byte for byte.
data.fonts#Fonts: Lato Regular, Bold, Black and italics and Roboto Mono Regular, Bold and italics are embedded, so gaia’s headings get their weight and italic text renders italic.
data.line-numbers#Line numbers:
In v0.8.0 a block can number its lines. Marp Core has no line numbers, and it ignores what follows a fence’s language, so the options go in braces there and a deck that uses them renders in Marp as it would without:
```go {lineNumbers} func main() { fmt.Println("hello") } ``` ```go {lineNumbers=10} // starts at 10 ``` Write Means {lineNumbers} number from 1 (Slidev’s {lines:true} and Pandoc’s {.numberLines} are read too) {lineNumbers=10} number from 10 (also startLine=10, Pandoc’s startFrom="10") {lineNumbers=false} no numbers, whatever the slide says For every block of a slide and the slides after it, set the directive: (_lineNumbers for one slide). A kind can set it once for a family of slides:
kinds: listing: {lineNumbers: true} Each number starts its line inside the theme’s code box, set apart by a rule. It stays on its line’s baseline even when the line is taller, for example with a callout or an emoji. The numbers are muted by a colour mixed from the code’s colour and its background, with 4.5:1 contrast or more in the default, gaia and uncover themes, light and dark. They are not selectable in the page and are not read by screen readers. In a PDF they are drawn but left out of the text, so a text extractor reads the code alone. In a PowerPoint or OpenDocument file they are editable text at the start of each line. A deck that does not use the option renders as before, to the byte. Highlighting chosen lines is not supported yet.
data.math#Math:
$…$ is an inline formula and $$…$$ a display formula:
The famous one is $E=mc^2$, and this is a display formula: $$ \int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} $$ The delimiter rules are Marp Core’s, read from marp-core 4.4.0: a $ followed by a space does not open a formula, and one followed by a digit does not close it, so prices such as $5 and $10 stay text. go-tex/math typesets each formula into inline SVG sized in em, so it follows the text’s size and sits on its baseline. The same SVG is used in the HTML page, in images and in the PDF. A formula that does not parse stays visible as written; the error is kept in its title.

data.why-it-is-fast#Why it is fast: No browser to start. marp-cli launches Chrome for every PDF, image and PPTX export; go-slides renders with go-webengine inside its own process. Fonts are parsed once per process, not once per slide.

data:
Open the playground →
The playground is go-slides itself, v0.13.0, compiled to WebAssembly and running in your browser. Type a deck on the left; the slides follow on the right. Nothing is sent to a server: not the deck, not a share link.
data.security#Security:
The deck is shown in an iframe sandboxed without the page’s origin: it can reach neither the playground nor its storage, submit no form and navigate nothing. Its page carries a Content Security Policy that runs only its own scripts. Raw HTML in the deck follows Marp’s allowlist, as slides does by default. A render that runs for more than 5 seconds (a template that loops) is stopped.
The presenter window keeps that sandbox. It is opened by the playground itself and shows the deck in an iframe sandboxed the same way. The two iframes cannot share storage, so the playground relays the slide number between them in messages. No frame that runs the deck gets the playground’s origin.
The project’s media reach the sandboxed frames as bytes in a message, and each frame makes its own blob: URLs of them, in its own origin. A blob: URL made by the playground does not load there, and the frames’ policy gains only blob: for media and fonts.
The playground can be served from your own machine, behind a sign-in: see Self-hosting.
data.size-and-speed#Size and speed: The module is 8.8 MiB as GitHub Pages serves it (gzip; Pages does not serve brotli). It is downloaded once with a progress bar, then cached by the browser until the next deploy. On an Apple M4 Max with Chrome 155, measured against the live page, the editor is ready 2.1 s after the page opens, 1.5 s of which is the download, and the first slides appear at 2.4 s. A change to the 100-slide benchmark deck reaches the preview in about 30 ms: go-slides renders only the slides that changed, and only those are replaced in the preview.
data.what-it-has#What it has:
Live preview of every slide, rendered off the page’s thread (a Web Worker), so typing never waits for it. Click a slide to move the editor to its line; move the caret and the preview scrolls to its slide.
Slideshow: the presentation itself, with the keyboard, the on-screen controller and the transitions.
Presenter view: Present (or p in the slideshow) opens it in a second window: the current slide, the next step, the speaker notes (the deck’s ), a clock and a timer. The arrow keys, Space, Home and End work in either window, and each follows the other, also when you edit the deck. If the window does not open, allow pop-ups for the site. The overview view (o) is in the downloaded page only.
Completion as you type: directive keys (spot _ ones in comments), the values of kind, theme, size, paginate, and template functions and data fields inside {{ }}.
Help for what is under the caret: a directive, a kind (what it sets), a template function. The help pane also links to these pages.
Problems on their line: template, YAML and HCL errors are highlighted in the editor and listed under it, and the preview keeps the last deck that rendered.
Examples: a welcome deck, templates that generate slides, slide kinds, an HCL front matter, themes and spot directives, and math, images and backgrounds (![bg], a split ![bg left:40%], filters).
Files: the panel left of the editor is the deck’s project, laid out the way the command and the VS Code extension read it: deck.md, slides.yaml, themes/, kinds/, media/.
Click a file to edit it. The editor colours it by its language (Markdown, YAML, HCL, JSON, CSS) and marks its problems. Right-click (or Shift+F10) for New File, New Folder, Rename (F2), Delete (asks first) and New theme / New kind. Drag a file onto a folder to move it. The keyboard follows the WAI-ARIA tree pattern, type-ahead included. Project ▸ New theme makes themes/my-gaia.css (or from default, uncover): @import of the built-in theme and the rules you add. It joins the Theme list. New kind and New data file start from templates too. Each is listed in slides.yaml, so slides build deck.md finds it. Project ▸ Download project (.zip) saves it all. Unzipped, slides build deck.md builds it. Open project takes a .zip or a folder back. An archive that leaves its folder (.., absolute paths), holds more than 256 files or 8 MiB in a file, or inflates more than 100 times is refused. Everything is kept in this browser with the draft. A project holds up to 64 MiB, and the line under the files says how much is used. Media: drop or paste an image, a video or a sound on the editor and it goes into media/, and the deck names it: ![](media/photo.png). Drop files on a folder of the panel to put them there. The deck stays small and readable, and nothing is uploaded. The preview’s sandbox loads them without being opened up (the page hands it the bytes). Save as ▸ HTML page puts them in the page. https: images work too, but the browser fetches them from their server, which then sees your address. The preview sends no referrer.
Resizable panes: the file panel, the editor, the slide thumbnails, the preview and the help are separated by bars you can drag (the pointer becomes a resize cursor over one). The pane beside the bar takes the room, the others keep their size. Double-click a bar, or press Enter on it, to pull the pane shut and bring it back. From the keyboard, F6 moves between the bars, the arrow keys move one by 16 px, Home and End take the pane before it to its smallest and largest, and Escape returns to the editor. The View tab still switches panes off. The sizes you set are kept in this browser, with the draft; the default sizes (190, 168 and 280 px, the editor and the preview sharing the rest 6 to 5) are never stored.
Format: the Format tab edits the Markdown for you, and each press is one step of Undo.
Text: Bold, Italic, Strikethrough and Inline code work on the selection or the word at the caret and toggle (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+Shift+X and Ctrl+E; Cmd on a Mac). A button shows pressed when the caret is inside its marks. Markdown has no underline: Underline (Ctrl+U) wraps the text in …, a tag Marp’s default HTML allow-list keeps, so it works with raw HTML off. Paragraph: Heading 1 to 3 (Ctrl+Alt+1..3), bullets (Ctrl+Shift+8), numbering (Ctrl+Shift+7) and a quote work on the selected lines and toggle. The horizontal rule is the tag: ---, *** and ___ would each start a new slide in Marp. Table: a grid picks the columns and rows. At the caret in a table you add or remove a row or a column and align the column (:--, :-:, --:); the table is rewritten aligned after each edit. Slide text left, centre or right writes a

data: The playground is static files, and slides --server is one process on the loopback. Both can run on your own machine, behind your own name, for people who sign in with your organisation’s account. This page does it with Caddy (tested with v2.11.7), which obtains and renews the HTTPS certificates itself, and oauth2-proxy for the sign-in. Every file shown here is in selfhost/, and its CI checks each Caddyfile with caddy validate.
data.caddyfile#Caddyfile:
slides.example.org is your name. Its A and AAAA records point at the machine, and ports 80 and 443 reach Caddy:
import headers.caddy slides.example.org { root * /srv/go-slides-site file_server { precompressed br gzip } import playground_headers } caddy run --config Caddyfile.playground The playground is then at https://slides.example.org/playground/.
data.check-it#Check it: curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' 'https://slides.example.org/playground/playground.wasm?v=v0.1.0' The answer says content-type: application/wasm, content-encoding: br and cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, with the content-security-policy above. With the sign-in in front, the same request without a cookie answers 302 to /oauth2/sign_in.
data.references#References: Caddy: automatic HTTPS, file_server, header, reverse_proxy, forward_auth. RFC 8555, ACME: HTTP-01 (8.3), DNS-01 (8.4). OpenID Connect Core 1.0: the authorization code flow (3.1), the redirect URI (3.1.2.1), the ID Token (2). oauth2-proxy: configuration, OpenID Connect provider.
data.sign-in-with-openid-connect#Sign-in with:
Caddy asks oauth2-proxy about every request (forward_auth). oauth2-proxy answers 202 for a browser that has signed in, which Caddy then serves, and 401 otherwise, which Caddy turns into a redirect to the sign-in. The sign-in is the authorization code flow of OpenID Connect Core 1.0: the browser goes to your provider (Keycloak, Authentik, Entra ID, Google, Okta, Dex…), comes back to /oauth2/callback with a code, oauth2-proxy exchanges the code for an ID Token, checks it, and sets its own cookie.
Register a client with your provider, confidential, with the authorization code flow. Its redirect URIs, which must match exactly: https://slides.example.org/oauth2/callback and https://decks.example.org/oauth2/callback. Put the secrets in files readable by oauth2-proxy alone: the client’s secret, with no newline at the end, and a cookie secret of exactly 32 random bytes (head -c 32 /dev/urandom). Your secret store writes them (systemd credentials, Docker or Kubernetes secrets, Vault…); neither goes into a configuration file, a command line or an environment variable, where logs and ps show them. Configure oauth2-proxy (oauth2-proxy.cfg): http_address = "127.0.0.1:4180" reverse_proxy = true trusted_proxy_ips = ["127.0.0.1/32", "::1/128"] upstreams = ["static://202"] set_xauthrequest = true provider = "oidc" oidc_issuer_url = "https://id.example.org/realms/example" client_id = "go-slides" client_secret_file = "/run/secrets/oauth2-proxy-client-secret" code_challenge_method = "S256" redirect_url = "/oauth2/callback" whitelist_domains = ["slides.example.org", "decks.example.org"] email_domains = ["example.org"] cookie_secret_file = "/run/secrets/oauth2-proxy-cookie-secret" cookie_secure = true cookie_samesite = "lax" redirect_url without a host brings each site’s sign-in back to its own callback, so each site keeps its own cookie. whitelist_domains is where a sign-in may return to: asked to go anywhere else, it stays on your site. trusted_proxy_ips believes the X-Forwarded-* headers from Caddy alone. email_domains says who may come in; oauth2-proxy also has options for groups and lists of addresses.
Configure Caddy (Caddyfile.oidc): import headers.caddy (signed_in) { handle /oauth2/* { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4180 } handle { forward_auth 127.0.0.1:4180 { uri /oauth2/auth copy_headers X-Auth-Request-User X-Auth-Request-Email @unauthorized status 401 handle_response @unauthorized { redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={scheme}://{hostport}{uri} 302 } } {block} } } slides.example.org { import signed_in { root * /srv/go-slides-site file_server { precompressed br gzip } import playground_headers } } decks.example.org { import signed_in { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 } } slides -s --allowed-host decks.example.org /srv/decks oauth2-proxy --config /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy.cfg caddy run --config Caddyfile.oidc oauth2-proxy and slides listen on the loopback only: the one way in is through Caddy, and so through the sign-in. The playground’s headers go inside the signed-in block, on the playground alone: oauth2-proxy’s sign-in page is a form, which their form-action 'none' would stop.
The alternative is caddy-security, a Caddy module that does the sign-in inside Caddy, with no second process. It needs a Caddy built with the module (xcaddy), and its own configuration language.
data.slides---server-behind-the-proxy#slides:
slides --server stays on 127.0.0.1 and Caddy forwards to it. The server checks the Host header of each request and the Origin of each live reload’s WebSocket, against DNS rebinding and other sites’ pages, and the proxy keeps the public name in both. --allowed-host adds that name to what the checks accept; they stay on:
slides -s --allowed-host decks.example.org /srv/decks decks.example.org { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 } The live reload goes through as it is (Caddy proxies WebSockets without configuration). Do not use --host 0.0.0.0 for this: it serves the directory to the whole network, around the proxy and its sign-in.
--allowed-host comes after v0.13.0. Until the next release, install the commit that has it: go install github.com/go-slides/slides/cmd/slides@v0.13.1-0.20261026090714-2e1da79f663e.
data.the-playground#The playground:
Each release of the site attaches the whole site, playground included, as one tarball built for the root of a domain, with its SHA-256:
curl -fLO https://github.com/go-slides/go-slides.github.io/releases/download/v0.1.0/go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz curl -fLO https://github.com/go-slides/go-slides.github.io/releases/download/v0.1.0/go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz.sha256 sha256sum -c go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz.sha256 tar -xzf go-slides-site-v0.1.0.tar.gz -C /srv mv /srv/go-slides-site-v0.1.0 /srv/go-slides-site The tarball is reproducible: building the same tag again gives the same bytes. Beside every file that compresses (the WebAssembly modules, the fonts, the pages, the scripts) it carries the same file compressed with Brotli (.br) and gzip (.gz), so the server sends them as they are and compresses nothing on the fly.
data.what-the-server-must-get-right#What the:
HTTPS. Caddy gets the certificate from Let’s Encrypt with ACME (RFC 8555), proving that it holds the name by answering on port 80 (HTTP-01) or 443 (TLS-ALPN-01), and renews it. A machine that the CA cannot reach can use the DNS-01 challenge instead (a TXT record, which needs a Caddy built with your DNS provider’s module), or your own certificate with tls cert.pem key.pem. On a test machine, tls internal uses Caddy’s local CA. application/wasm. Caddy sends this type for .wasm; another server may need to be told. The playground compiles its modules from the bytes it has read (the export engine as it downloads, in a response of its own with that type), so it starts even from a server that sends another type; with nosniff, the right type is still the one to send. Compression. precompressed br gzip sends playground.wasm.br to a browser that accepts Brotli, .gz to one that accepts gzip, and the file itself otherwise, with Vary: Accept-Encoding. The editor’s module is about 7 MiB in Brotli, against 33 MiB uncompressed. Caching. The page asks for every module, worker, font and picture with the release in the query (playground.wasm?v=v0.1.0), so those can be kept for a year (immutable). The pages themselves are revalidated (no-cache): a new release is seen at the next visit. The headers in headers.caddy: (playground_headers) { header { Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; worker-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https:; img-src 'self' data: blob: https:; media-src 'self' data: blob: https:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https:; font-src 'self' data: blob: https:; frame-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'" X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Referrer-Policy no-referrer Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" } @versioned query v=* header @versioned Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" @unversioned not query v=* header @unversioned Cache-Control "no-cache" } The policy is the one the playground needs: its scripts (the loader is inline), its WebAssembly ('wasm-unsafe-eval') and its worker, all from your server. A deck’s pictures, style sheets and fonts may come from any https: address, as they do in the command’s output; drop https: from img-src, style-src, font-src, media-src and connect-src to keep every request on your server, and decks that point elsewhere show without those resources. The deck itself runs in iframes sandboxed without your origin, under a stricter policy of their own that the playground writes into each frame: it cannot reach the playground, its storage or your cookies, whatever this header says. frame-ancestors 'self' stops other sites from framing the playground.
No COOP or COEP. The playground uses neither SharedArrayBuffer nor threads, so it does not need to be cross-origin isolated. Sending Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp would block a deck’s pictures from other sites.
data.without-the-network#Without the network: Once the page is loaded, everything happens in the browser: the editor, the preview, the presenter view, and the PDF, PPTX and ODP exports, whose fonts are in the tarball. The deck is sent neither to your server nor anywhere else. What needs the network is what the deck names: pictures or style sheets at an https: address, and the gaia theme’s web font, which it asks of fonts.bunny.net (without it, the slides fall back to another font). The links to this documentation leave your server.

data: The deck is a Go text/template, evaluated before the Markdown is parsed. Everything the Go template language has — actions, pipelines, if, range, with, variables — works in a deck.
data.code-is-left-alone#Code is left alone: Fenced code blocks and inline code spans are set aside before the template runs and restored verbatim, so a slide about Go templates can show {{ .Name }} without escaping it.
data.data#Data:
The template’s dot holds the front matter’s keys, then the keys of its data: mapping, then the data given on the command line or in slides.yaml — each overriding the one before.
--- marp: true title: Quarterly review data: team: Platform --- # {{ .title }} Presented by the {{ .team }} team. From the command line:
Flag Gives --data file.yaml a YAML or JSON file of data (repeatable) --set key=value one value (repeatable)
data.generating-slides#Generating slides:
The whole body is one template, so a range that writes --- writes slides:
{{ range .releases }} --- # {{ .version }} {{ range .changes }}- {{ . }} {{ end }} {{ end }}
data.include#Include: {{ include "parts/agenda.md" }} inserts another file, relative to the deck.
data.page-and-total#Page and total: {{ page }} and {{ total }} are the slide’s number and the number of slides. They are known only once the deck has been split, so they are filled in then — a generated deck counts the slides it generated.
data.turning-it-off#Turning it off: --no-template reads the deck as plain Marp: {{ is text.

data: The extension is go-slides/vscode, versioned on its own (v0.4.0). It renders with go-slides v0.9.0 (the editor package, the source lines of scroll sync, and the overview and presenter view). It is installed from the go-slides-0.4.0.vsix attached to its GitHub release: its publication on the VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX is prepared, but it is not there yet. The extension is go-slides’ counterpart of Marp for VS Code: the deck shows in VS Code’s Markdown preview as slides, its errors in the Problems panel, and directives, kinds and template functions complete as you type.
data.export#Export: go-slides: Export Slide Deck… (also in the editor’s title bar) writes HTML, vector PDF, editable PPTX and ODP, PNG or JPEG with the slides command, as slides -o deck.pdf deck.md would; see Command line. It needs a trusted workspace. If slides is not found, the extension offers to run the go install above in a terminal.
data.in-v071-and-extension-v022#In v0.7.1 and:
go-slides v0.7.1 caches parsed themes, packed style sheets and highlighted code between renders, marks scroll-sync lines without going byte by byte, and reuses its writers: a render of the 100-slide deck allocates 5.7 MB, against 52.7 MB for extension v0.2.0. With it, extension v0.2.2 drops the GOGC=400 override. For comparison, extension v0.2.1 took 72 ms for the first preview and 44 ms after an edit at the default GOGC (36 ms with GOGC=400), and v0.2.0 took 47–51 ms.
Extension v0.2.2 measured 52 ms for the first preview and 24 ms after an edit, level with Marp’s 23 ms.
data.in-v080-and-extension-v030#In v0.8.0 and: go-slides v0.8.0 keeps each open deck’s rendered slides and, after an edit, re-renders only those whose source or inherited state changed (directives, page number, total, heading ids, link references, source lines); the output is the same as a full render, byte for byte. Typing in slide 50 of 100 re-renders one slide: 2.5 ms natively, 11.5 ms in WebAssembly. VS Code’s preview then morphs only the changed slide’s DOM, and the extension’s smoke test types one character into slide 50 between timed renders, for both extensions. The extension’s presenter view syncs through the parent window (postMessage).
data.install#Install:
Download go-slides-.vsix from the releases, then run Extensions: Install from VSIX…, or:
code --install-extension go-slides-0.4.0.vsix The preview needs nothing else. Exporting needs the slides command:
go install github.com/go-slides/slides/cmd/slides@latest
data.performance#Performance:
On go-slides’ 100-slide benchmark deck, in VS Code 1.142 on an Apple M4 Max, with Marp for VS Code 3.6.1 measured in the same session:
go-slides Marp for VS Code activation (loading the WebAssembly module) 189 ms — first preview 52 ms 78 ms preview after an edit (median) 19 ms 23–24 ms .vsix 7.5 MB 36.3 MB The figures are for extension v0.3.0 (go-slides v0.8.0) on a 100-slide deck, typing one character into slide 50, from interleaved rounds under a 1-minute load below 8. The first preview is faster than Marp’s, and the preview after an edit is now faster than Marp’s too.
data.presenting#Presenting:
Since v0.4.0 of the extension (go-slides v0.9.0), a deck can be presented without leaving VS Code. With the deck in the editor, from the Command Palette or the editor’s … menu:
Command Opens go-slides: Open Overview a panel with every slide in a grid. A chosen slide shows its source in the editor; Esc closes the panel go-slides: Start Presenter View the slides, and beside them the presenter view: the next step, the speaker’s notes and a timer The panels sit beside the editor and follow one another: change slide in one and the others change with it. They also follow your edits to the deck. The p key in the slides opens the presenter view.
To present on another screen, move the slides panel there with View: Move Editor into New Window.
Each panel runs the deck in a sandboxed frame (no allow-same-origin) under a policy of default-src 'none': the frame loads images, media, styles and fonts and nothing else, and runs only the scripts go-slides built into the page, named by hash. A script the deck wrote does not run.
data.preview#Preview:
Open a deck and Markdown: Open Preview to the Side. A deck is a Markdown file whose front matter says slides: true:
--- slides: true paginate: true data: who: World --- # Hello {{ .who }} --- # Page {{ page }} of {{ total }} Files with marp: true are previewed too, unless Marp for VS Code is installed: both extensions would render the same document. The setting goSlides.preview.marpDocuments decides: auto (the default), always or never.
The preview is go-slides itself, compiled to WebAssembly and loaded by the extension: no binary, and it works on vscode.dev. It reads what the deck uses from the workspace — slides.yaml or slides.hcl next to the deck, the kinds files they name, files a template includes, theme CSS — and only from the deck’s workspace folder.
data.problems-completion-hover#Problems, comp: Problems: template, YAML and HCL errors, on the line they are on, in the deck or in the kinds file they come from. Completion: directive keys in the front matter and in comments (with _ for a spot directive), the values of kind and _kind (with what each kind sets), theme, size, paginate, math, headingDivider; inside {{ }}, the template functions and the data fields. data.scroll-sync#Scroll sync:
Since v0.2.0 of the extension (go-slides v0.7.0), the editor and the preview scroll together, both ways, as they do for plain Markdown: the preview follows the slide and the block under the editor’s cursor, and scrolling the preview moves the editor. The settings are VS Code’s own, markdown.preview.scrollPreviewWithEditor and markdown.preview.scrollEditorWithPreview.
Lines are traced through templates. A slide that a {{ range }} generates follows the line of its template, and what an {{ include }} brings in follows the include’s line. A deck split by headingDivider syncs on its headings.
data.security#Security: The deck and the workspace are untrusted. Raw HTML follows Marp’s allowlist unless goSlides.html is on in a trusted workspace (a slides.yaml with html: true does not turn it on in the preview), and VS Code’s preview runs no script from the deck. The preview reads files of the deck’s workspace folder only, follows no symbolic link, and templates see no environment variable. Exporting runs a program, so it waits for workspace trust, and the program is never named by the workspace.
data.settings#Settings: Setting Default goSlides.cliPath "" the slides command; empty: slides on PATH. A machine setting: a workspace cannot set it goSlides.exportType pdf the format the export dialog proposes first goSlides.exportAutoOpen true open the exported file goSlides.html false allow all raw HTML instead of Marp’s allowlist; honoured only in a trusted workspace goSlides.preview.marpDocuments auto preview marp: true decks: auto, always, never
